title: Probable Chikungunya case
symptoms_or_prerequisites: severe arthralgia/arthritis not explained by other medical conditions
residing or having visited epidemic areas
reported transmission within 15 days prior to onset

requires_all.value: transmission within 15 days prior to onset

recommended_action: Classify as probable case and consider confirmatory testing

source.title: NATIONAL GUIDELINE ON CLINICAL MANAGEMENT OF CHIKUNGUNYA FEVER

evidence.passage: Probable case: a patient meeting both the clinical and epidemiological criteria

title: Laboratory confirmation of Chikungunya
symptoms_or_prerequisites: viral RNA by real‑time RT‑PCR (within 5 days of onset)
viral specific IgM antibody (5‑28 days of onset)
four‑fold rise of IgG antibody (samples ≥3 weeks apart)
recommended_action: Obtain appropriate laboratory test based on days since symptom onset to confirm case

source.title: NATIONAL GUIDELINE ON CLINICAL MANAGEMENT OF CHIKUNGUNYA FEVER

evidence.passage: Laboratory Criteria: at least one of the following tests in the acute phase: Virus isolation by Cell Culture; Presence of viral RNA by real Time RT‑PCR (Within 5 days of onset of Illness); Presence of viral specific IgM antibody in single serum sample collected within 5 to 28 days of onset Fever; Four‑fold Rise of IgG antibody in samples collected at least three weeks apart (1st sample after 7 days )

title: Chikungunya fever clinical diagnosis
recommended_action: Diagnose chikungunya fever when the typical combination of fever lasting 24‑48 hours with abrupt onset (up to 39‑40 °C) and the joint manifestations described (symmetric arthralgia/arthritis affecting ankles, wrists, small hand joints, possibly migratory polyarthritis) are present, especially if accompanied by any of the listed infrequent or rare features.

source.title: NATIONAL GUIDELINE ON CLINICAL MANAGEMENT OF CHIKUNGUNYA FEVER

evidence.passage: The fever varies from low grade to high grade, lasting usually for 24 to 48 hours. Fever rises abruptly in some, reaching 39-400C, with chills and rigor, no diurnal variation, usually subsides with use of antipyretics.

The joint symptoms usually start with arthralgia or arthritis. Involvement is symmetric and often ankles wrists and small joints of the hand are the worst affected. Migratory polyarthritis with effusions may be seen, but resolves in the majority.

Table 1: Clinical features of Chikungunya fever ... Common: Fever, Arthritis/Arthralgia, Backache, Headache, Rash ... Infrequent: Stomatitis, Oral ulcers, Exfoliative dermatitis, Photosensitive, hyperpigmentation ... Rare in adults but seen in children: Photophobia, Retro-orbital pain, Vomiting, Diarrhoea, Mental confusion, Signs of meningeal irritation

title: Transient maculopapular rash
recommended_action: Consider chikungunya fever as a likely diagnosis when a transient maculopapular rash appears and disappears within 48 hours.

source.title: NATIONAL GUIDELINE ON CLINICAL MANAGEMENT OF CHIKUNGUNYA FEVER

evidence.passage: Transient maculopapular rash is commonly seen, usually disappear within 48 hours.

recommended_action: Evaluate for neurologic complications and refer to neurology if present

Neurologic manifestation
Neurologic  manifestations  of  meningo-encephalitis,   encephalitis,  acute

title: Ocular Manifestations of Chikungunya
recommended_action: Perform ophthalmologic examination; most patients recover with good vision

source.title: NATIONAL GUIDELINE ON CLINICAL MANAGEMENT OF CHIKUNGUNYA FEVER

evidence.passage:
Ocular manifestation
Neuro-retinitis and uveitis in one or both eyes may occur. The main ocular
manifestation associated with the recent epidemic outbreak of chikungunya
virus infection in South India included granulomatous and nongranulomatous
anterior  uveitis,  optic  neuritis,  retrobulbar  neuritis, and  dendritic  lesions.
Majority of the patients recover with good vision.

symptoms_or_prerequisites: GI bleeding due to use of drugs e.g. analgesics
Shock due to persistent vomiting and diarrhoea
recommended_action: Classify patient as having severe chikungunya and initiate appropriate supportive care and monitoring

source.title: NATIONAL GUIDELINE ON CLINICAL MANAGEMENT OF CHIKUNGUNYA FEVER

evidence.passage:
Severe
  Persistent high grade fever
  Severe arthralgia/Arthritis
  Persistent vomiting / Diarrhoea
  Altered sensorium
  Bleeding (GI bleeding due to use of drugs e.g. analgesics)

title: High‑Risk Chikungunya Patients
symptoms_or_prerequisites: Co‑morbid condition (Hypertension, Diabetes, CAD/CVD, Geriatric age, Pregnancy, COPD)
Co‑infection (Dengue, Tuberculosis, Enteric fever, Pneumonia, HIV, Malaria)
recommended_action: Identify patient as high‑risk for complications and consider closer monitoring and early intervention

source.title: NATIONAL GUIDELINE ON CLINICAL MANAGEMENT OF CHIKUNGUNYA FEVER

evidence.passage:
High Risk group

Chikungunya infection with one of the following conditions may be considered as high risk.

a) Co-morbid condition

Hypertension, Diabetic, CAD/CVD, Geriatric age, Pregnancy, COPD,

b) Co-infection

Dengue, Tuberculosis, Enteric fever, Pneumonia, HIV, Malaria

title: Expected Clinical Course of Chikungunya
recommended_action: Inform patient that acute symptoms usually resolve within 7–10 days; advise that rheumatologic relapses may occur months later and to seek follow‑up if they develop polyarthralgia, polyarthritis or tenosynovitis

source.title: NATIONAL GUIDELINE ON CLINICAL MANAGEMENT OF CHIKUNGUNYA FEVER

evidence.passage:
Clinical course and outcome
  Acute symptoms typically resolve within 7–10 days
 Some patients might have relapse of rheumatologic symptoms (e.g., polyarthralgia, polyarthritis, tenosynovitis) in months following acute illness

title: Chikungunya fever
recommended_action: Consider chikungunya fever as the primary diagnosis in patients presenting with fever and joint pain, recognizing that joint pain may persist for months to years.

source.title: NATIONAL GUIDELINE ON CLINICAL MANAGEMENT OF CHIKUNGUNYA FEVER

evidence.passage: In variable proportions of patients, joint pain may persist for months to years.

title: Consider differential diagnoses for febrile arthralgia

variants.action: Consider dengue fever; confirmatory laboratory diagnosis is possible.
Consider reactive arthritis; hallmark feature is enthesitis and oral mucosal ulcers may be seen.
Consider serum sickness illness; may be associated with polyarthritis.
Consider rickettsial disease; confirm by serology.
Consider rheumatic fever; use Modified Jones criteria and check ASO titre and sore throat history.

recommended_action: Evaluate for alternative diagnoses based on specific clinical features such as severe backpain with purpura, enthesitis, rash, or migratory polyarthritis.

source.title: NATIONAL GUIDELINE ON CLINICAL MANAGEMENT OF CHIKUNGUNYA FEVER

evidence.passage: Some of the diseases which can be considered in differential diagnosis are:
(1) Dengue fever: Severe backpain with purpuras or active bleeding might suggest dengue fever. Confirmatory laboratory diagnosis is possible.

(2) Reactive Arthritis: In general, any arthritis that follows a febrile gastrointestinal or genitourinary infection ... is considered a reactive acute inflammatory arthritis if it lasts less than six months. The hallmark feature is enthesitis ... Oral mucosal ulcers are seen.
(3) Serum sickness illness: Polyarthritis may be associated with a serum sickness type reaction caused by vaccine, medication or other viral infections
(4) Rickettsial disease can present with fever, rash and joint pains. Confirm by serology.

(5) Rheumatic fever: More common in the children and presents with fleeting (migratory) polyarthritis predominantly affecting the large joints. Modified Jones criteria should be the basis for diagnosis. Raised ASO titre and a history of recurrent sore throat are other points to be noted.

title: Chikungunya fever
recommended_action: Consider chikungunya as the likely diagnosis when fever >38.5°C and prominent arthralgia are present, especially if the pattern of other features (arthritis, headache, rash, myalgia, lymphopenia) matches the typical chikungunya profile.

source.title: NATIONAL GUIDELINE ON CLINICAL MANAGEMENT OF CHIKUNGUNYA FEVER

evidence.passage:
Fever (>38.5°C)    +++            ++
Arthralgia        +++                  +/-
Arthritis         +                        -
Headache        ++             ++
Rash            ++             +
Myalgia          +              ++
Lymphopenia      +++            ++

title: Paracetamol for fever in suspected chikungunya
recommended_action: Take paracetamol tablets during periods of fever

medication.name: Paracetamol
medication.dose: 1000 mg per dose up to four times daily for adults; 50-60 mg/kg per day divided for children
medication.frequency: up to four times daily as needed for fever
medication.instructions: Do not exceed recommended daily dose; avoid if liver or kidney disease present

source.title: NATIONAL GUIDELINE ON CLINICAL MANAGEMENT OF CHIKUNGUNYA FEVER

evidence.passage: Take paracetamol tablets during periods of fever (up to 1000 mg tablets four times daily), in persons with no preexisting liver or kidney disease. Children may be given 50-60 mg per kg body weight per day in divided doses.

title: Hydration for mild/moderate chikungunya at home
recommended_action: Consume approximately 2 litres of home‑available fluids with salt in 24 hours

source.title: NATIONAL GUIDELINE ON CLINICAL MANAGEMENT OF CHIKUNGUNYA FEVER

evidence.passage: Consume plenty of water with electrolytes (approximately 2 litres of home available fluids with salt in 24 hours).

title: Rest and joint care during acute chikungunya
recommended_action: Adequate rest in a warm environment; avoid heat, use cold compresses on joints; refrain from exertion; mild exercise and physiotherapy recommended during recovery

source.title: NATIONAL GUIDELINE ON CLINICAL MANAGEMENT OF CHIKUNGUNYA FEVER

evidence.passage: Adequate rest in a warm environment
Cold compresses may help in reducing joint damage. Heat may increase/worsen joint pain and is therefore best to avoid during acute stage.
Refrain from exertion. Mild forms of exercise and physiotherapy are recommended in recovering persons.

title: Avoid NSAIDs and aspirin until dengue ruled out
recommended_action: Do not use aspirin or other NSAIDs because they can increase hemorrhage risk if dengue is present

source.title: NATIONAL GUIDELINE ON CLINICAL MANAGEMENT OF CHIKUNGUNYA FEVER

evidence.passage: Aspirin and other NSAIDs can increase the risk of hemorrhage in patients with dengue
Patients with suspected chikungunya should be managed as dengue until dengue has been ruled out

title: Avoid aspirin and NSAIDs
recommended_action: Do not use aspirin or non‑steroidal anti‑inflammatory drugs for chikungunya fever

source.title: NATIONAL GUIDELINE ON CLINICAL MANAGEMENT OF CHIKUNGUNYA FEVER

evidence.passage: Avoid self medication with aspirin or NSAIDs.

source.title: NATIONAL GUIDELINE ON CLINICAL MANAGEMENT OF CHIKUNGUNYA FEVER

evidence.passage: Antihistamines can be used for itching.

recommended_action: Start appropriate antibiotics

recommended_action: Recommend mild forms of exercise and physiotherapy in recovering persons

title: Avoid aspirin and NSAIDs in acute phase
recommended_action: Avoid aspirin or NSAIDs during first 10 days; NSAIDs may be used only after dengue fever is adequately excluded

source.title: NATIONAL GUIDELINE ON CLINICAL MANAGEMENT OF CHIKUNGUNYA FEVER

evidence.passage: Aspirin or NSAIDs should be avoided during first 10 days. NSAIDs can be used in Chikungunya only when Dengue fever is adequately excluded.

recommended_action: Do not use steroids in the acute stage of Chikungunya

source.title: NATIONAL GUIDELINE ON CLINICAL MANAGEMENT OF CHIKUNGUNYA FEVER

evidence.passage: Steroid has no role in acute stage.

title: Ophthalmic symptom referral
recommended_action: Consult with ophthalmologists for ophthalmic symptom complications

source.title: NATIONAL GUIDELINE ON CLINICAL MANAGEMENT OF CHIKUNGUNYA FEVER

evidence.passage: In cases with ophthalmic symptoms complications, consult with ophthalmologists.

title: Bleeding disorder management
recommended_action: Provide platelet transfusions; consider fresh frozen plasma or Vitamin K if INR >2

source.title: NATIONAL GUIDELINE ON CLINICAL MANAGEMENT OF CHIKUNGUNYA FEVER

evidence.passage: Bleeding disorders with blood components- platelet transfusions in case of bleeding with platelet counts of less than 50,000 cells per cu mm., fresh frozen plasma, or Vitamin K injections if prothrombin time INR is more than 2.

title: Anti-neuralgic drugs for neuropathic pain
recommended_action: Use standard doses of anti-neuralgic drugs

source.title: NATIONAL GUIDELINE ON CLINICAL MANAGEMENT OF CHIKUNGUNYA FEVER

evidence.passage: Anti-neuralgic drugs (Amitryptyline, Carbamazepine, Gabapentin, and Pregabalin) can be used in standard doses in disturbing neuropathies.

title: Hydroxychloroquine or chloroquine for refractory arthralgia
recommended_action: Use hydroxychloroquine or chloroquine phosphate for four weeks

source.title: NATIONAL GUIDELINE ON CLINICAL MANAGEMENT OF CHIKUNGUNYA FEVER

evidence.passage: Use hydroxychloroquine 200 mg orally once daily or chloroquin phosphate 300 mg orally per day for a period of four weeks in cases where arthralgia is refractory to other drugs.

title: Topical treatment for hyperpigmentation and papular eruptions
recommended_action: Apply zinc oxide cream and/or calamine lotion

source.title: NATIONAL GUIDELINE ON CLINICAL MANAGEMENT OF CHIKUNGUNYA FEVER

evidence.passage: Hyperpigmentation and papular eruptions can be managed with Zinc oxide cream and/or Calamine lotion.

title: Specimen collection for chikungunya diagnosis
recommended_action: Collect blood or serum for testing; collect CSF if neurological features are present

source.title: NATIONAL GUIDELINE ON CLINICAL MANAGEMENT OF CHIKUNGUNYA FEVER

evidence.passage:
Preferred Specimen:
1) Blood or Serum
2) CSF (if neurological features present)

title: Routine laboratory investigations for chikungunya
recommended_action: Order CBC, ESR, and C‑Reactive Protein

source.title: NATIONAL GUIDELINE ON CLINICAL MANAGEMENT OF CHIKUNGUNYA FEVER

evidence.passage:
Routine Laboratory Investigations
    CBC
      o Leucopenia (Decreased WBC)
      o Thrombocytopenia: rare
      o ESR: Usually Elevated
     C-Reactive Protein: Increased during the Acute Phase and may remain elevated for a week

title: Breastfeeding guidance for mothers with perinatal chikungunya infection
symptoms_or_prerequisites: mother with chikungunya infection in perinatal period (−4 to +1 days around delivery)
recommended_action: Encourage mother to breastfeed; transmission via breast milk not reported

source.title: NATIONAL GUIDELINE ON CLINICAL MANAGEMENT OF CHIKUNGUNYA FEVER

evidence.passage: Mothers are encouraged to breast feed their infants.

title: Potential vertical transmission of chikungunya in perinatal period
symptoms_or_prerequisites: maternal chikungunya infection occurring −4 to +1 days around delivery
recommended_action: Consider vertical transmission; monitor neonate for fever, poor feeding, pain, distal edema, skin manifestations, seizures, meningo‑encephalitis, echocardiographic abnormalities

source.title: NATIONAL GUIDELINE ON CLINICAL MANAGEMENT OF CHIKUNGUNYA FEVER

evidence.passage: Mothers afflicted with Chikungunya fever in the perinatal period (−4 days to +1 days before/after delivery) can transmit Chikungunya fever to neonates by vertical transmission.

recommended_action: Perform at least one specific laboratory test in the acute phase

source.title: NATIONAL GUIDELINE ON CLINICAL MANAGEMENT OF CHIKUNGUNYA FEVER

evidence.passage: Virus isolation by Cell Culture
Presence of viral RNA by real Time RT-PCR (Within 5 days of onset of Illness)
Presence of viral specific IgM antibody in single serum sample collected within 5 to 28 days of onset Fever
Four-fold Rise of Ig G antibody in samples collected at least three weeks apart (1st sample after 7 days )

title: RT‑PCR testing for Chikungunya
recommended_action: Send sample for real‑time RT‑PCR (performed only at IEDCR)

source.title: NATIONAL GUIDELINE ON CLINICAL MANAGEMENT OF CHIKUNGUNYA FEVER

evidence.passage: Presence of viral RNA by real Time RT-PCR (Within 5 days of onset of Illness)

title: Public health measures to prevent Chikungunya transmission
recommended_action: Implement risk communication, reduce vector population, and minimize vector‑patient contact (Aedes bite during daytime, especially morning and late afternoon)

source.title: NATIONAL GUIDELINE ON CLINICAL MANAGEMENT OF CHIKUNGUNYA FEVER

evidence.passage:
Minimizing transmission of  infection:   This can be done  in  the following ways:
      o  Risk communication to the household members
      o  Minimize the vector population
      o  Minimize the vector-patient contact (Aedes mosquitoes  bite during day time, mostly in the morning and late afternoon)

title: NSAID prescription in post‑acute chikungunya

requires_all.note: afebrile period of at least 48 hours

recommended_action: Prescribe NSAID

source.title: NATIONAL GUIDELINE ON CLINICAL MANAGEMENT OF CHIKUNGUNYA FEVER

evidence.passage: After 7-10 days of acute phase, NSAID can be prescribe by physician if dengue is excluded (NS1 antigen for Dengue is negative, afebrile period of atleast 48 hours and no warning or danger sign of dengue)

title: Cold compression in acute chikungunya
recommended_action: Advise cold compression and maintain normal joint movement

source.title: NATIONAL GUIDELINE ON CLINICAL MANAGEMENT OF CHIKUNGUNYA FEVER

evidence.passage: The experts agreed that there is no indication of physiotherapy in acute phase. Only cold compression can be advised. Maintain normal movement of joints and body.

title: Mild exercise in post‑acute chikungunya
recommended_action: Recommend mild exercises such as walking on level ground, active hand movements and proper joint posturing

source.title: NATIONAL GUIDELINE ON CLINICAL MANAGEMENT OF CHIKUNGUNYA FEVER

evidence.passage: Mild forms of exercise are recommended in post-acute phase a. Exercises like walking on level grounds, active hand movements and proper posturing of joints to avoid stiffness must be suggested.

title: Referral to arthralgia clinic in chronic phase
symptoms_or_prerequisites: persistent joint pain after acute phase
recommended_action: Advise patient to attend arthralgia clinic for specialist consultation

source.title: NATIONAL GUIDELINE ON CLINICAL MANAGEMENT OF CHIKUNGUNYA FEVER

evidence.passage: Patients who are suffering for joint pains (arthralgia and arthritis) after acute phase, can be advised to go to arthralgia clinics in hospitals in chronic phase and arthralgia clinic will consult with specialists of physical medicine.

title: Physiotherapy referral for disabled/elderly/athlete patients
symptoms_or_prerequisites: loss of physical fitness or autonomy

variants.action: Consider consulting a physical medicine specialist

recommended_action: Consider consulting a physical medicine specialist and refer to physiotherapist if needed

source.title: NATIONAL GUIDELINE ON CLINICAL MANAGEMENT OF CHIKUNGUNYA FEVER

evidence.passage: Consulting a physical medicine specialist may be considered for patients with loss of physical fitness and of autonomy (disabled and/or elderly patients, athletes) to implement a specific rehabilitation program.
